```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 96)
```

WSVAflowR calibrates several streamflow models on the same gauge, with the
same climate forcing and the same tests, so you can compare them fairly and
then drive all of them with a different climate. This vignette runs the
whole workflow on a basin that ships with the package, so nothing is
downloaded.

```{r setup}
library(WSVAflowR)
options(wsva.data_dir = file.path(tempdir(), "wsva"))   # where caches go (default: a per-user cache folder)
```

## A basin

A `wsva_basin` holds a watershed, its daily flow, climate forcing and basin
attributes. `example_basin()` is Clear Creek above Clear Creek Reservoir in
Colorado: a 174 km² snowmelt basin whose gauge is operated by the Colorado
Division of Water Resources (CDSS station `CCACCRCO`).

```{r basin}
b <- example_basin()
b
```

For your own gauge, the same object comes from a few calls (they need
network access; see `vignette("your-flow-data")`):

```{r, eval = FALSE}
b <- wsva_basin_usgs("01154000")            # a USGS gauge, or
b <- wsva_basin(flow_cdss("CCACCRCO"))      # a Colorado DWR gauge, or
b <- wsva_basin(flow_from_csv("q.csv", q_col = "Q", lon = -105.3, lat = 40.0))
b <- add_forcing(b)                         # GridMET basin-mean climate
b <- add_basin_attributes(b)                # terrain, soils, rain/snow threshold, land cover
```

Before fitting, `check_basin()` looks for problems that would make results
misleading: too short a record, a watershed that disagrees with the
published drainage area, a runoff ratio that suggests imported water or bad
precipitation, and flow that may be affected by people.

```{r checks}
check_basin(b)
```

## Fit the models

`fit_models()` calibrates each model with DDS on KGE and evaluates it three
ways:

* **Blocked cross-validation.** The record is cut into 5 blocks of whole
  water years; each block is predicted by a model calibrated on the
  others. This gives an honest skill score and a continuous out-of-sample
  series.
* **Climate-contrast test.** Calibrate on the wettest (or driest, coolest,
  warmest, earliest) third of the years and test on the opposite third: a
  check on how a model transfers to a different climate.
* **Full-record calibration.** One parameter set fit on every year, used
  by `predict()` to run the model with new forcing.

The default budget is 1,000 model runs per calibration. This vignette uses
100 and three of the five models to stay quick; results are cached, so
re-running a fit only recomputes what changed.

```{r fit}
fits <- fit_models(b, models = c("wbm", "gr4j", "hbv"), n_evals = 100)
fits
```

## Skill

```{r summary}
s <- summary(fits)
s
```

`kge`, `nse` and `log_nse` are medians over the five held-out blocks
(`log_nse` weights low flows); `pbias` is the percent bias (positive means
the model under-predicts). The **model mean** averages the models' daily
flows and is often better than any one of them. The **DOY climatology** is
a benchmark that just predicts each calendar day's average flow: a model
has to beat it to be adding anything. In a regular snowmelt basin like this
one it is a strong benchmark for low flows (compare `log_nse`), even though
the models beat it easily on overall KGE.

```{r skill-plot, fig.height = 3, fig.alt = "Test-fold KGE, NSE and log-NSE for each model, with the median marked"}
plot(fits, type = "skill")
```

```{r overview, fig.height = 9, fig.alt = "Observed and out-of-sample simulated flow for each model: recent hydrographs on linear and log scales, flow duration curves, mean monthly flow and annual flow"}
plot(fits)
```

## Transfer to a different climate

The second table in the summary, and the plot below, come from the
climate-contrast test. Models that keep their skill and, above all, their
water balance (small bias) when calibrated in one climate and tested in
another are the safer choice for projections.

```{r contrast, fig.height = 3.5, fig.alt = "KGE and percent bias for each model when calibrated in one climate extreme and tested in the opposite"}
plot(fits, type = "contrast")
```

## Run the models with a different climate

`predict()` with new forcing runs every model with its full-record
parameters. PET is recomputed from the new temperature, humidity,
radiation and wind with the same Penman-Monteith method used in
calibration. A simple sensitivity test: 2 °C warmer and 10% less
precipitation than the historical record.

```{r predict}
hist <- b$forcing
warm_dry <- transform(hist, tmin_c = tmin_c + 2, tmax_c = tmax_c + 2, tmean_c = tmean_c + 2,
                      prcp_mm = prcp_mm * 0.9)
q0 <- predict(fits, forcing = hist)
q1 <- predict(fits, forcing = warm_dry)

models <- c("wbm", "gr4j", "hbv", "mean")
change <- sapply(models, function(m) 100 * (mean(q1[[m]], na.rm = TRUE) / mean(q0[[m]], na.rm = TRUE) - 1))
round(change, 1)   # percent change in mean flow
```

The models agree on the direction but not the size of the change. That
spread is part of the uncertainty in any projection, and the reason for
running several models rather than one.

```{r monthly, fig.height = 3.5, fig.alt = "Change in mean monthly flow for each model under 2 degrees warmer and 10 percent drier forcing"}
month <- factor(month.abb[as.integer(format(q0$date, "%m"))], levels = month.abb[c(10:12, 1:9)])
monthly <- function(q) sapply(models, function(m) tapply(q[[m]], month, mean, na.rm = TRUE))
d <- as.data.frame(as.table(monthly(q1) - monthly(q0)))
names(d) <- c("month", "model", "change_mm_day")
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(d, aes(month, change_mm_day, color = model, group = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey60") + geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Change in mean flow (mm/day)", color = NULL,
       title = "+2 °C, -10% precipitation: change in mean monthly flow") +
  theme_minimal()
```

With climate projections, the same call runs each model on each climate
model's historical and future forcing; comparing the two runs of the same
climate model gives the projected change.

## Parameters

```{r coef}
head(coef(fits), 10)
```

```{r params, fig.height = 6, fig.alt = "Calibrated parameter values as a fraction of their bounds, one point per cross-validation fold"}
plot(fits, type = "params")
```
